summary: The paper runs a fully controlled, from-scratch comparison of three cheap LLM uncertainty signals (token-level predictive entropy, semantic entropy, self-consistency) on a synthetic arithmetic task with exact ground truth, across 5 training seeds with bootstrap CIs and paired significance tests. It finds token entropy has the highest point-estimate AUROC in 5/5 seeds, but after applying Holm-Bonferroni correction across all 10 per-seed pairwise tests, zero survive at family-wise alpha=0.05, and even the sign test supporting the direction-of-effect claim is shown to be fragile to a single seed flipping. The paper's main contribution is methodological: demonstrating, via its own three-revision history, how single-seed point estimates, single-reference-seed significance tests, and uncorrected multi-seed win-counts can each look convincing until subjected to proper multiple-comparison correction and fragility analysis, ultimately landing on a null result under honest correction.
strengths:
- The statistical practice is unusually careful for this class of work: per-seed bootstrap paired tests, reporting the full p-value distribution rather than a single reference seed, an explicit Holm-Bonferroni correction across all 10 tests, and a fragility check on its own sign test (showing p=0.031 becomes p=0.19 under a single seed flip) — this is exactly the kind of self-scrutiny the introduction's cited KDD survey (Xiao et al. 2025) says is typically missing from this literature.
- All numbers I checked are internally consistent: I cross-referenced every reported statistic (per-seed AUROCs, per-seed p-values, medians 0.122/0.032, Holm-Bonferroni threshold 0.05/10=0.005 vs. smallest raw p=0.007, sign-test values 0.03125/0.1875, correlation r=0.15353, elapsed_seconds=563.19) against results_summary_v2.json and run_output.log, and they match exactly, and raw_results_v2.json contains exactly the claimed 400 held-out records for the reference seed.
- The paper is transparent about its own limitations and revision history (including a previously shipped runtime artifact that had drifted from the reported number), and the conclusion's claims (a family-wise null, a fragile sign test, an unexplained digit-length reversal) are calibrated to what the results actually show rather than oversold.
- Full code, raw per-example outputs, and aggregate statistics are released, and the experimental setup (exact-match clustering, exact ground truth) removes major confounders (retrieval, human labeling, pretraining exposure) present in prior large-model studies.
weaknesses:
- The experimental scope is extremely narrow: a single ~300K-parameter model family, one synthetic arithmetic task, and only 5 seeds. The paper is explicit about this, but it means the central claim ('a small number of from-scratch seeds is not enough to declare one signal better than another') is really a demonstration of low statistical power rather than a finding that generalizes to the open-domain-QA settings (Farquhar et al. 2024) that motivated the comparison — the paper acknowledges this gap only as future work, not as a limitation on how far the current conclusion can be read.
- I was unable to re-execute experiment.py in this sandboxed environment (python/node execution was blocked), so verification is limited to static/artifact-level consistency (the shipped JSON, log, and text all agree) rather than an independent from-scratch reproduction; the paper's own history of a previously drifted artifact makes this a relevant, if now-addressed, class of risk.
- The contribution is primarily methodological/cautionary rather than a new signal, method, or dataset — as a case study it is well-executed, but the underlying empirical finding (three cheap signals separated by only a few AUROC points, indistinguishable at n=400 with 5 seeds) is a fairly expected outcome of a small controlled setting and does not by itself advance understanding of why token entropy wins on this task or whether the pattern would hold with more seeds or larger models.
- The digit-length stratification reversal (1-digit answers) and the accuracy/advantage correlation (r=0.15) are both explicitly flagged as underpowered/inconclusive by the authors, which is appropriate, but it means two of the paper's secondary analyses contribute little beyond 'more seeds needed' — a conclusion already reached from the primary correction analysis.
questions:
1. Given that Future Work estimates ~110s/seed, why not simply run enough additional seeds (e.g., 20-30) within this same controlled setup to get a Holm-Bonferroni-corrected test with real power, rather than leaving that as future work — the paper's own numbers suggest this would cost well under an hour of CPU time?
2. Do the authors have any hypothesis for why token entropy's advantage concentrates in 2- and 3-digit answers but reportedly flips for 1-digit answers (n=37), beyond noting it as underpowered — e.g., does greedy decoding become less informative when there are fewer plausible completions (single-digit answers) or is this simply sampling noise at n=37?
3. Since the model and task are fully synthetic and controlled, could exact reproducibility (bitwise-identical AUROCs across independent re-runs on the same hardware/software stack) be verified and reported, given that the paper already flags a prior runtime-artifact mismatch as a caution about reproducibility hygiene?
